paper_title: MOSS: Self-Evolution through Source-Level Rewriting in Autonomous Agent Systems

questions.question: What deployment problem motivates MOSS?
questions.expected_answer: Deployed agents are mostly static, so failures seen in real interactions can keep recurring until a human ships an update.

questions.question: What limitation do the authors identify in earlier self-evolving agent systems?
questions.expected_answer: They change text-level artifacts such as prompts or skills, but leave the agent harness and its source code unchanged.

questions.question: Why can prompt edits fail to fix a harness-level routing problem?
questions.expected_answer: Prompt edits affect what the model thinks or says, while routing and other harness decisions are made by code outside that text layer.

questions.question: Why do the authors call source-level adaptation a more general medium?
questions.expected_answer: Because source code is Turing-complete and can express changes beyond the narrower set of text-configurable agent behaviors.

questions.question: How does source-level adaptation differ from prompt changes in how reliably changes take effect?
questions.expected_answer: Code changes execute deterministically, while prompt-based changes depend on whether the language model follows the edited text.

questions.question: What long-context issue do the authors say source-level changes avoid?
questions.expected_answer: Prompt and skill guidance can lose influence as context grows, whereas behavior implemented in code does not need to be reread as guidance each turn.

questions.question: What does MOSS do at a high level?
questions.expected_answer: It evolves a production agent by proposing source changes from real failure evidence, testing candidate builds, and promoting a successful candidate with user approval.

questions.question: What are the two paths by which failure evidence enters a MOSS batch?
questions.expected_answer: A periodic scan of session logs and a user-triggered flag for a dissatisfied conversation turn.

questions.question: What happens to session chunks that score weak or missing?
questions.expected_answer: They are added to the open failure batch for that conversation.

questions.question: What is the default chunk threshold for sealing an open batch?
questions.expected_answer: The default threshold is eight chunks.

questions.question: Who performs source edits, and what does MOSS retain control over?
questions.expected_answer: A pluggable external coding-agent CLI edits the code; MOSS controls stage ordering, verdicts, loop termination, and promotion timing.

questions.question: Why does the coding-agent CLI run on the host rather than inside the main container?
questions.expected_answer: The host provides the shell environment, network access, and scoped mounts needed for editing.

questions.question: What five main components make up the MOSS system?
questions.expected_answer: The user-facing main container, control CLI, external coding-agent CLI, host daemon, and temporary trial workers.

questions.question: Which commands are exposed through the MOSS control CLI?
questions.expected_answer: The nine commands are status, batches, batch, start, stop, restart, apply, flag, and catch-up.

questions.question: What are the seven stages in one MOSS evolution iteration?
questions.expected_answer: Locate, Plan, Plan-Review, Implement, Code-Review, Task-Evaluate, and Verdict.

questions.question: What does the Locate stage produce?
questions.expected_answer: It diagnoses the baseline traces and batch failures without proposing a fix.

questions.question: How are candidate task results scored in Task-Evaluate?
questions.expected_answer: Four to seven keypoints per task are rated on a qualitative scale from strong to missing.

questions.question: What does the plateau guard do?
questions.expected_answer: If no keypoint improves for several iterations, it stops further trials and converges at the best-scoring candidate so far.

questions.question: Why does MOSS use trial workers instead of relying only on code review?
questions.expected_answer: Runtime failures such as races, cross-module state problems, and hook-order issues may not be visible from inspecting a diff.

questions.question: How are trial workers isolated from the live agent?
questions.expected_answer: They run in short-lived containers without the live user-state mount and with isolated networking.

questions.question: Does a CONVERGED verdict automatically deploy the candidate?
questions.expected_answer: No. The system marks it ready, but the user must explicitly request the apply operation.

questions.question: What happens if the new container fails its health probes?
questions.expected_answer: The host daemon rolls back to the last-known-good image and reports the outcome.

questions.question: How does MOSS preserve a user's sessions during a container swap?
questions.expected_answer: User state is stored on a host-mounted volume that remains intact when the container image is replaced.

questions.question: What agent and underlying model were used in the case study?
questions.expected_answer: The evaluated system was OpenClaw using DeepSeek V3.2.

questions.question: What happened to the four-task mean grader score after one evolution cycle?
questions.expected_answer: It increased from 0.2526 before evolution to 0.6100 afterward.

questions.question: What kinds of tasks were used in the case study?
questions.expected_answer: Four English and Chinese compliance-audit tasks covered SLA violations and failures in multi-service restock chains.
